paragraphs: This paper studies portfolio selection when trading costs matter and the investor wants to hold only a limited number of assets. Its model balances returns against transaction costs while imposing a K-sparse constraint: at most K portfolio entries can be nonzero. Combining these goals addresses a gap in models that treat trading costs and sparse holdings separately.

The sparsity constraint makes the problem NP-hard. The authors reformulate it as a nonsmooth difference-of-convex optimization problem and prove equivalence when the penalty parameter is sufficiently large. They develop a proximal subgradient algorithm for this reformulation, using ADMM to compute the proximity operation needed to handle the objective and portfolio constraints.

The theoretical contribution establishes convergence of the entire sequence of iterates and an R-linear convergence rate from any starting point, using properties of a surrogate function. These are convergence guarantees, not a claim that every run finds the global optimum of the original hard problem. Tests on four real-market datasets report lower risk while maintaining higher returns than classical transaction-cost models.
icml-2026-a-linearly-convergent-proximal.tldr: The paper combines sparse portfolio holdings and transaction costs in an optimization method with proven linear convergence and favorable results on four market datasets.

paragraphs: Belief propagation performs distributed inference by passing information through a probabilistic graph. Representing the resulting probability distributions can become expensive in both computation and memory. Gaussian belief propagation reduces this burden by treating distributions as locally Gaussian, and it often works well even when the underlying problem contains strongly non-Gaussian relationships.

The paper asks when that approximation has a theoretical justification in sparsely connected graphs containing loops. Using the Central Limit Theorem, the authors prove that the beliefs associated with variables converge toward Gaussian distributions when the graph and inference process satisfy four key assumptions. The guarantee is therefore conditional on those assumptions, rather than applying to every sparse graph.

A stereo depth estimation experiment provides empirical support: variable beliefs become increasingly Gaussian after only a few belief-propagation iterations. The significance is that Gaussian behavior can emerge during inference even in a non-Gaussian problem. This offers a theoretical explanation for some of Gaussian belief propagation’s practical success in spatial inference, alongside evidence from a concrete vision task.
icml-2026-belief-propagation-converges-t.tldr: Under four stated assumptions, belief propagation produces increasingly Gaussian variable beliefs in sparse, loopy graphs, helping explain the usefulness of Gaussian approximations.

paragraphs: Generating a SQL query is only part of enterprise data engineering; developers must also diagnose and repair complex queries that fail. This paper introduces Squirrel Benchmark to evaluate that debugging ability. It separates syntax problems, where an explicit error message is available, from semantic problems, where the code does not accomplish the user’s intended task.

The benchmark uses an automated workflow that reverse engineers SQL and injects realistic bugs, making it possible to construct varied examples at scale. Its evaluation framework assesses repairs without executing the queries. Squirrel contains 469 syntax queries and 516 semantic queries, averaging more than 140 lines, with broad and deeply nested syntax trees that reflect substantial structural complexity.

Across nearly 30 evaluated models, the strongest reported model, Claude-4-Sonnet, reaches 36.46% accuracy on syntax debugging and 32.17% on semantic debugging; most models remain below 20%. These results show a substantial performance gap on the benchmark’s enterprise debugging tasks. The authors also investigate four solution strategies to identify difficulties and possible directions for improving this capability.
icml-2026-beyond-text-to-sql-can-llms-re.tldr: Squirrel Benchmark exposes major weaknesses in LLM debugging of complex enterprise SQL, with the best evaluated model solving roughly one-third of queries.

paragraphs: CAReDiO addresses how training data can help language models respond appropriately across different cultures. The authors identify two problems in existing culture-specific collections: they can repeat information while missing core cultural characteristics, and they can blur a culture’s distinctive nuances with patterns shared by other cultures. These problems concern both coverage and differentiation.

The framework improves the data by alternately refining culture-sensitive questions and their responses. It uses information-theoretic objectives within an in-context optimization process to increase how much cultural information the examples convey and how clearly they distinguish relevant cultures. This makes the choice and wording of training examples central to the alignment process.

Experiments across 15 cultures report richer cultural information and better alignment on both multiple-choice and open-ended benchmarks than previous datasets. The approach works with small open-source and large proprietary models, with successful alignment reported using as few as 200 training samples. The findings suggest that carefully improving cultural content can make a small dataset more useful, within the cultures and evaluations studied.
icml-2026-caredio-enhancing-cultural-ali.tldr: CAReDiO refines cultural training examples for coverage and distinctiveness, improving cultural alignment across 15 cultures with as few as 200 samples.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems distributed across a network, where participants must coordinate decisions involving both shared and local variables. The constraints are affine equalities, meaning they impose linear relationships with possible constant offsets. Different nodes can impose different constraints on global variables, while local variables face both node-specific restrictions and constraints coupling them together.

That combination captures coordination requirements found in federated learning, multi-task learning, resource allocation, and distributed control. The analysis covers smooth and nonsmooth objectives, as well as strongly convex and general convex cases. These distinctions matter because they change the mathematical structure available to an algorithm and the convergence rates that can be achieved.

The main result is an optimal algorithm for smooth, strongly convex objectives: its convergence rate matches established lower complexity bounds. Here, optimality concerns the algorithm’s rate relative to those bounds in that regime. For the other regimes, the authors provide optimal or near-optimal methods, extending the treatment beyond the most favorable objective assumptions.
icml-2026-complexity-of-decentralized-op.tldr: The paper develops optimal or near-optimal decentralized optimization methods for convex problems with interacting local and global affine equality constraints.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why giving a language model more factual training material can leave its memorization capacity underused. It frames factual learning in information-theoretic terms and empirically finds suboptimal accuracy when the information contained in training facts exceeds model capacity. Uneven fact frequencies worsen the gap between the capacity limit and the best accuracy realized across dataset sizes.

The proposed response is to select training data using training loss alone. The selection schemes aim to reduce the number of facts the model must absorb while making their frequencies more balanced. This addresses both the overall information burden and the concentration of repeated exposure on some facts, rather than assuming that retaining every training example maximizes useful memorization.

On semi-synthetic datasets containing high-entropy facts, selection raises fact accuracy to the capacity limit. In pretraining on annotated Wikipedia, a 110-million-parameter GPT2-Small model memorizes 1.3 times as many entity facts as standard training and matches a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained on the full dataset. That comparison concerns entity-fact memorization, rather than overall language-model capability.
icml-2026-cram-less-to-fit-more-training.tldr: Selecting training data to limit factual overload and balance fact frequencies improves memorization, allowing a smaller model to match a much larger model on entity facts.

paragraphs: The paper develops a mathematical framework for understanding gradient flow, the continuous-time description of gradient-based learning, in large learning problems. It expresses the changing loss as a formal power series whose coefficients are represented by diagrams resembling Feynman diagrams. The authors show that this expansion has a well-defined limit as problem size grows.

They apply the framework to learning Canonical Polyadic decompositions of high-order tensors. The analysis reveals several distinct learning regimes, including free evolution, neural tangent kernel behavior, and under- and over-parameterized mean-field behavior. Which regime appears depends jointly on parameter scaling, tensor order, and model symmetry, so size alone does not determine the learning dynamics.

The authors also introduce a way to sum the formal loss expansion by translating it into a partial differential equation. Across a wide range of scenarios, this equation is first-order and can be solved using the method of characteristics. The approach yields explicit nonlinear gradient-flow solutions in some cases, and the paper reports very good agreement between theoretical predictions and experiments.
icml-2026-gradient-flow-through-diagram-.tldr: Diagram-based expansions reveal distinct gradient-flow learning regimes and yield explicit solutions for some large tensor-learning problems.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover a directed acyclic causal graph through continuous optimization when nonlinear relationships include additive noise. Existing guarantees often assume equal noise scales or a known noise distribution. The authors address arbitrary noise in additive noise models, including settings where non-Gaussian noise with varying scales makes mean-squared-error approaches fail to identify the true graph.

Building on NOTIME, the method minimizes a criterion measuring dependence among residuals, the parts left unexplained by the fitted relationships. The authors show that a global minimizer recovers the underlying graph up to extra constant edges. That qualification matters: optimizing independence can identify the causal structure while still retaining edges that do not express meaningful functional dependence.

To remove those extra edges, the method uses an adaptive group lasso penalty on entire columns of a neural network’s first-layer weights. Grouping weights this way enables pruning that reflects a variable’s functional contribution. Experiments across different noise types and variances report stable, effective performance and improvements over prior methods lacking identifiability guarantees in this setting.
icml-2026-identifiable-nonlinear-differe.tldr: The method combines residual independence with adaptive group sparsity to recover nonlinear additive-noise causal graphs across varied noise distributions.

paragraphs: The linear assignment problem asks for an optimal matching between two sets. Exact solvers preserve optimality but face a cubic scaling bottleneck, while neural approximations can struggle to remain both scalable and exact. This paper uses learning to provide a better starting point for an exact solver by predicting its dual variables, which guide the optimization search.

Its RowDualNet architecture processes rows independently, avoiding the quadratic memory bottleneck associated with graph-based models and supporting neural warm-starts up to N = 16,384. A mechanism called Min-Trick guarantees feasibility of the predicted starting information by construction, removing the need for iterative projection. A fallback mechanism preserves worst-case guarantees when using the learned initialization.

The method reduces search effort in the Jonker-Volgenant solver while retaining strict optimality. Reported end-to-end speedups exceed 2 times on complex synthetic data, reach 1.25 times on real-world tracking, and reach 1.5 times on transportation networks. The experiments also report robust zero-shot generalization, showing that learned initialization can accelerate exact optimization across the tested settings.
icml-2026-learning-augmented-scalable-li.tldr: RowDualNet predicts feasible starting information that speeds up exact assignment solving while preserving optimality and worst-case guarantees.

paragraphs: Multimodal models often learn separate representations for each input type and then combine them to make predictions. This paper examines why that setup can struggle when recording conditions change. The authors identify fusion overfitting: joint training encourages encoders to exploit relationships between modalities that are specific to the training environment, rather than learning features that remain useful across environments.

MER-DG addresses this failure mode by maximizing the entropy of each encoder’s feature distribution. The aim is to preserve a diverse set of features within each modality, countering the narrowing associated with dependence on source-specific cross-modal patterns. The regularizer is added to the training loss and can be incorporated into different multimodal architectures.

Experiments on EPIC-Kitchens and HAC report average improvements of approximately 5% over standard fusion and approximately 2% over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support feature diversity as a useful intervention for multimodal domain generalization in the evaluated settings. The contribution includes both an explanation of a training failure and an architecture-agnostic way to address it.
icml-2026-mer-dg-modality-entropy-regula.tldr: MER-DG preserves diversity in each modality’s features to reduce fusion overfitting and improve generalization to new recording conditions.

paragraphs: Language-model performance depends strongly on the information and instructions available at inference time. Context engineering tries to improve those inputs, but its own procedures are often manually fixed. This paper argues that predefined schemas and rigid generation-and-reflection workflows restrict the range of context designs an agent can discover.

Meta Context Engineering uses two levels of optimization to evolve both the context and the skills used to construct it. A meta-level agent improves engineering skills through agentic crossover, searching over previous skills, their executions, and evaluations. A base-level agent applies those skills, learns from training rollouts, and develops context in flexible forms such as files and code.

Across five domains in offline and online settings, MCE reports relative improvements of 5.6–53.8% over state-of-the-art agentic context-engineering methods, averaging 16.9%. The authors also report stronger adaptability, transferability, and efficiency in context use and training. The central finding is that improving the process for designing context can add value beyond optimizing context within a fixed process.
icml-2026-meta-context-engineering-via-a.tldr: Meta Context Engineering jointly evolves context-building skills and context artifacts, improving performance across five evaluated domains.

paragraphs: MM-DeepResearch targets agents that must plan searches, invoke multiple tools, and combine visual and textual evidence. The authors identify three development obstacles: too few multimodal questions that genuinely require searching, insufficient examples of successful search sequences, and the expense of reinforcement learning through online search APIs. Their framework addresses each obstacle with a separate component.

Hyper-Search generates question-answer pairs using a hypergraph that connects visual and textual nodes within and across modalities. These connections support questions requiring different search tools. DR-TTS then organizes tasks by tool type, optimizes specialized tool experts, and combines those experts through tree search to produce successful sequences of searches for complex tasks.

An offline search engine supplies multiple search tools during reinforcement learning without relying on costly online search APIs. Together, the data generation, trajectory construction, and offline training components produce the MM-DeepResearch agent. The paper reports superior results across benchmarks. Its contribution links the ability to learn multimodal research behavior with the availability of suitable questions, successful tool-use examples, and an affordable training environment.
icml-2026-mm-deepresearch-a-simple-and-e.tldr: MM-DeepResearch combines multimodal question generation, tool-expert search trajectories, and offline search training to improve research-agent performance.

paragraphs: Any-to-any modeling aims to predict one modality from any combination of other modalities using a single network. This paper explores a decoder-only approach to that goal. The motivation is that common encoder-decoder and diffusion approaches are typically trained from scratch, preventing them from using strong pretrained decoder-only models as a starting prior.

MODUS treats modalities symmetrically: every modality can serve as both input and output within the same model. It does so without separate modality-specific heads, losses, or task pipelines. This shared formulation makes it possible to reuse one model for different directions of prediction instead of organizing each direction as a separate task-specific system.

That symmetry also supports chained generation through intermediate modalities and cross-modal self-verification, where another generated modality helps score the model’s outputs. Across several benchmarks, MODUS reports strong out-of-the-box performance and competitiveness with specialist and multitask baselines. The findings show that a single decoder-only model can support diverse multimodal prediction roles while enabling these additional ways to generate and assess outputs.
icml-2026-modus-decoder-only-any-to-any-.tldr: MODUS uses one decoder-only model for symmetric any-to-any multimodal prediction, enabling chained generation and cross-modal self-verification.

paragraphs: Instruction-based image editing can produce strong results, but users often have to decide which changes to request and in what order. PhotoAgent takes on that planning work. It interprets a user’s aesthetic intent and treats editing as a sequence of decisions whose combined effects determine the final image, without requiring step-by-step prompts from the user.

The system uses tree search to plan multiple editing actions and then refines the result through closed-loop execution. Memory and visual feedback inform subsequent decisions, allowing the process to respond to the edited image rather than relying only on an initial plan. Explicit aesthetic planning connects the user’s broad goal to an evolving sequence of concrete edits.

For evaluation, the authors introduce UGC-Edit, comprising 7,000 photos and a learned aesthetic reward model, along with a 1,017-photo test set. Across diverse editing scenarios, experiments report significant improvements over existing methods in both instruction faithfulness and visual quality. The findings support combining planning with feedback when assessing autonomous editing against both user intent and appearance.
icml-2026-photoagent-exploratory-visual-.tldr: PhotoAgent plans and revises multi-step image edits using visual feedback, improving instruction faithfulness and visual quality in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper investigates prompt injection as a failure to distinguish who is speaking. Although model inputs carry role labels, the authors find that models can infer authority from how text sounds. Untrusted content that imitates a trusted source can therefore be represented internally as though it came from that source, creating a route for instructions to cross trust boundaries.

The authors build role probes to measure this internal perception. They also introduce CoT Forgery, a zero-shot attack that places fabricated reasoning in user prompts or tool outputs. In their experiments, models mistake the injected reasoning for their own thoughts, and the attack reaches 60% success against frontier models where baseline success is near zero.

The measured degree of role confusion predicts attack success before the model generates its response. The authors also observe the mechanism in standard agent prompt injections, extending the analysis beyond fabricated reasoning. The contribution is a measurable account of how role imitation can influence behavior, linking internal representations of a text’s source to observed attack outcomes.
icml-2026-prompt-injection-as-role-confu.tldr: The paper links prompt-injection success to measurable role confusion, where models internally treat untrusted text as the trusted source it imitates.

paragraphs: This paper studies a form of image memorization centered on recurring layouts and visual structures. The authors call these template-memorized images. Their concern is that an image generator can reproduce memorized visual content through ordinary-looking prompts, even when the person prompting it has little or no access to the training data.

The proposed reconstruction attack requires few resources and does not depend on carefully engineered prompts or extensive training-set access. In one reported example, a simple request for a blue unisex T-shirt reproduces visual content depicting a real individual. The observation raises the possibility that users without adversarial intent could unintentionally reconstruct memorized content during plausible everyday use.

The authors also observe interpolation phenomena in template memorization. These findings raise questions about how to judge the novelty of generated images and whether established memorization detectors capture this form of reproduction effectively. The paper’s contribution is to demonstrate an accessible reconstruction pathway and characterize behavior that extends beyond straightforward extraction of an obviously memorized image.
icml-2026-reconstructing-template-memori.tldr: Ordinary-looking prompts can reconstruct template-memorized visual content with few resources and little or no training-data access.

paragraphs: A policy with high average returns can still expose an agent to rare, severe failures. RiskZero addresses this issue in the MuZero family of model-based reinforcement-learning methods. It learns how to plan without prior knowledge of the environment’s dynamics while making risk sensitivity an explicit part of the decision process.

The method learns distributional quantities that estimate risk over entire trajectories, rather than judging actions only by expected return. These estimates guide search toward policies that avoid rare but damaging outcomes. The authors establish theoretical convergence to optimal stationary risk-sensitive policies, connecting the search procedure to a defined risk-sensitive objective rather than relying solely on empirical behavior.

Evaluation includes environments designed to test risk-sensitive learning from pixels and larger combinatorial tasks. Across the reported settings, RiskZero outperforms state-of-the-art risk-sensitive baselines and improves sample efficiency. The results support using learned trajectory-level risk estimates inside planning, showing benefits both in the quality of risk-sensitive decisions and in how efficiently the agent learns from experience.
icml-2026-riskzero-plan-more-to-risk-les.tldr: RiskZero learns trajectory-level risk estimates to guide model-based planning away from rare severe outcomes, with theoretical convergence and improved experimental performance.

paragraphs: RoCA addresses the difficulty of deploying an end-to-end driving model in environments different from those used for training, such as another city. The paper focuses on both generalization without target-domain adaptation and adaptation when a new domain is available. Its approach models uncertainty and relationships in driving representations through a joint probability distribution.

Specifically, RoCA models tokens encoding the ego vehicle and surrounding vehicles. Using a Gaussian process, it learns basis tokens and associated trajectories that span diverse driving scenarios. These learned elements support probabilistic inference of future trajectories from a driving scene, providing a structured way to connect scene representations with possible vehicle motion.

When used alongside a base driving model during source-domain training, RoCA improves that model’s generalization without adding inference computation. It also supports adaptation to target domains, where the authors report significant improvements over direct fine-tuning. Evaluations across multiple cross-domain scenarios show strong generalization and adaptation performance, supporting the use of probabilistic trajectory structure in training and adapting driving models.
icml-2026-roca-robust-cross-domain-end-t.tldr: RoCA uses probabilistic vehicle-token and trajectory modeling to improve cross-domain driving generalization and adaptation without extra inference computation for the trained base model.

paragraphs: Vision-and-language navigation requires an agent to follow language instructions while making fine-grained movements with only partial knowledge of its surroundings. The paper identifies a problem with open-loop execution: an agent’s internal state can drift without a mechanism for detecting and correcting that drift during inference. SC²-WM introduces feedback into this decision process.

The framework uses predictions from a world model to generate internal feedback. Before executing an action, the agent uses that feedback to refine its plan at the state level. This creates an opportunity to revise the internal basis for a decision before the decision becomes a movement in the environment.

For more challenging situations, the method also provides conditional adaptation of the world model itself. It selectively updates the model at test time when feedback indicates that its capacity is insufficient. These two forms of correction address the current plan and the model supporting it. Experiments on standard continuous-navigation benchmarks report better robustness and generalization, supporting the value of internal feedback during navigation.
icml-2026-sc-2-wm-a-self-correcting-worl.tldr: SC²-WM uses world-model feedback to refine navigation plans before acting and selectively adapt the model when feedback indicates insufficient capacity.

paragraphs: Transfer learning usually starts with a source dataset containing meaningful examples that can help a model learn a target task. This paper explores a surprising alternative: a synthetic source made from simple noise distributions. The setting is semi-supervised learning, where only a small fraction of target examples have labels and most are unlabeled.

The authors formalize this setting as Semi-Supervised Noise Adaptation. Their goal is to use the noise domain to improve generalization on the target domain. They first derive a generalization bound describing how the noise source affects target performance, then use that analysis to design a method called the Noise Adaptation Framework.

Experiments report that the framework uses the noise domain effectively, tightening the target-domain generalization bound and improving performance. The significance is that useful adaptation need not always begin with semantically meaningful source samples. In the studied semi-supervised setting, synthetic noise can play a productive role when incorporated through a framework grounded in an analysis of its effect on generalization.
icml-2026-semi-supervised-noise-adaptati.tldr: The Noise Adaptation Framework uses a synthetic noise source to improve semi-supervised target learning, guided by a generalization bound.

paragraphs: Image generators can be steered toward a downstream objective by searching for better initial noise while keeping model parameters fixed. The difficulty is that the noise space is large, and many changes to it have little effect on the final image. This paper examines why some search directions are more influential than others.

The authors identify a spectral bias: the generator’s sensitivity to initial perturbations falls rapidly as their frequency increases. Spectral Evolution Search uses that observation to restrict gradient-free evolutionary search to a low-frequency subspace. This concentrates the search on variations that the analysis indicates have greater influence on the generated result.

The paper derives a Spectral Scaling Prediction from the dynamics of perturbation propagation, explaining the frequency-dependent effect theoretically. Experiments across diverse settings report a substantially better trade-off between generation quality and computation, with consistent improvements over strong baselines at equal compute budgets. The findings support using the generator’s sensitivity structure to allocate inference-time search effort more effectively.
icml-2026-spectral-evolution-search-effi.tldr: Spectral Evolution Search improves reward-aligned image generation by focusing initial-noise search on influential low-frequency directions.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether time-series, image, and language models develop a shared representational structure. This extends a hypothesis usually studied in vision and language to a third modality. The authors first find that independently pretrained encoders have nearly orthogonal representation geometry when there is no explicit coupling between them.

They then freeze the encoders and train projection heads with contrastive learning to align their outputs. This setup lets them examine alignment while leaving the underlying encoders unchanged. Alignment improves with model size, but the relationships are asymmetric: time series align more strongly with images than with text, and images can serve as effective intermediaries between time series and language.

Increasing descriptive information also has diminishing benefits. Richer textual descriptions improve alignment up to a threshold, beyond which denser captions bring no further improvement; analogous effects appear for visual representations. These findings show that alignment depends on modality relationships and information characteristics as well as scale, offering concrete considerations for systems that combine time series with vision and language.
icml-2026-time-series-vision-and-languag.tldr: Explicit contrastive alignment connects time series, vision, and language unevenly, with images providing a stronger bridge and richer descriptions helping only up to a threshold.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Omni Dense Captioning, a task that turns video into detailed, timestamped narratives covering both sound and visual content. A six-dimensional structural schema organizes the captions into a script-like description of successive scenes. The goal is to preserve continuous, fine-grained meaning so that a reader can imagine how the video unfolds.

The authors build OmniDCBench with human annotations and introduce SodaM, an evaluation metric for detailed descriptions that accounts for timing while reducing ambiguity around scene boundaries. They also create the TimeChatCap-42K training dataset and train TimeChat-Captioner-7B through supervised fine-tuning and GRPO, using rewards designed for the captioning task.

Experiments report state-of-the-art captioning performance, including results above Gemini-2.5-Pro. The generated descriptions also significantly improve downstream audio-visual reasoning on DailyOmni and WorldSense and temporal grounding on Charades-STA. These findings give the captions two roles: a readable account of a video and a useful representation for subsequent tasks that require understanding events and locating them in time.
icml-2026-timechat-captioner-scripting-m.tldr: TimeChat-Captioner generates structured, timestamped audio-visual narratives that improve dense captioning and downstream video reasoning and grounding.

paragraphs: TimeMoDE addresses time-series generation when only a small amount of target-domain training data is available. It combines a Diffusion Transformer with a mixture of experts and pretrains on a large collection of datasets from multiple domains. This pretraining aims to learn both shared temporal structure and domain-specific information that can support later fine-tuning.

The framework uses Domain Prompts to guide expert assignment when noisy tokens are otherwise difficult to distinguish. This provides domain information for routing and helps represent relationships across datasets. It also supplies diffusion timestep signals, allowing experts to adjust to how degraded the time series is and to the denoising requirements of the current diffusion stage.

These mechanisms connect two kinds of adaptation: selecting expertise relevant to the data domain and adjusting that expertise to the stage of generation. Experiments across diverse low-data settings report improvements over existing methods. The results support transferring knowledge from broad pretraining while retaining domain and diffusion-stage information for few-shot time-series synthesis.
icml-2026-towards-a-unified-generative-m.tldr: TimeMoDE combines multi-domain pretraining with domain-guided and diffusion-stage-aware experts to improve time-series generation with scarce target data.

paragraphs: This paper uses graph connectivity to investigate why Transformers sometimes learn brittle shortcuts instead of generalizable algorithms. For a simplified architecture called the Disentangled Transformer, the authors prove that an L-layer model can compute connectivity on graphs with diameter up to 3^L. The resulting strategy is equivalent to computing powers of the adjacency matrix.

The training analysis connects learning behavior to whether most examples fall within that capacity. Graphs within the diameter bound drive learning toward the algorithmic strategy, while beyond-capacity graphs drive learning toward a simple node-degree heuristic. This distinguishes the model’s ability to represent an algorithm from the conditions under which training actually leads it to learn that algorithm.

Experiments show that the insight also applies to standard Transformers: restricting training graphs to remain within model capacity makes both standard and Disentangled Transformers learn the exact algorithm. The findings establish a concrete connection between training-data difficulty and algorithm learning in graph connectivity, with theoretical results for the simplified architecture and empirical evidence for the standard one.
icml-2026-transformers-provably-learn-al.tldr: For graph connectivity, training examples within a Transformer’s capacity encourage exact algorithm learning, while beyond-capacity examples encourage a node-degree shortcut.
